The two bets

Bet I — reach

Watch anything, via tools

Today a trigger must exist in a catalog (ours or Activepieces'). But a customer's tool isn't in any catalog. If our events only fire for apps we integrated, we're not event-driven — we're app-integrated. Let the agent turn its own tools into triggers.

Bet II — reach + run

Events with & without AP, in the cloud

Activepieces is one trigger backend — not the spine. Make the full event layer run with zero AP (native schedule / poll / tool-triggers), keep AP for the 754 managed SaaS connectors, and deploy both so it isn't a laptop demo behind a flaky tunnel.

Bet I is about what we can watch. Bet II is about how we run. They share one seam — /invoke — so neither disturbs the other.

Part I

Watching on tools

The agent doesn't just answer with a tool — it watches with one.

The gap — a catalog is someone else's world

Our push triggers map to a fixed registry: gmail/new_email, github/new_pr, box/new_file. Great — until the thing you want to watch is your internal ticketing API, a pricing service, a warehouse tool, an MCP server you wrote last week. None of those are in AP's 754, and never will be.

Today

"when a new email arrives…"

User names the app + event. We look it up in the trigger registry and arm an AP piece. Bounded by the catalog.

Where we're going

"tell me when a critical bug appears…"

No app named. The agent already has a bug tool. It figures out how to watch it, and fires when the world changes. Bounded only by the agent's tools.

The reframe — the agent authors the watcher

A tool-trigger isn't picked from a menu by a human. It's synthesized by the agent from the tools it holds. Three decisions, all the agent's:

DecisionExample — "watch for large refunds"
Which tool answers this? list_refunds() — the agent already carries it; no new integration.
How do we detect an event? poll every 10 min, keep refunds where amount > 5000, fire on any new id.
What counts as "new"? the refund id — the dedup key, so we never re-alert the same one.

This is the shift from human-authored triggers (name the app) to agent-authored triggers (state the intent). The tool surface becomes the trigger surface.

The one abstraction — a WatchSpec

At arm time the agent emits a small declarative spec. The LLM runs once (to author it); a deterministic poller runs it forever — no model call per tick, so it's cheap and stable.

# agent-authored at arm; executed deterministically thereafter
WatchSpec {
  tool:     "list_refunds",          # a tool the agent already holds
  args:     { "since": "{{cursor}}" },  # incremental if the tool supports it
  key:      "$.refunds[*].id",       # dedup identity → "is this new?"
  where:    "amount > 5000",          # optional predicate / threshold
  map:      { title: "$.customer", body: "$.amount" }, # → the /invoke envelope
  cadence:  "10m",                   # user-overridable; floor enforced
  engine:   "poll"                    # or "subscribe" / "agent" (next slides)
}

Same discipline as pieces: a tool-trigger is DATA, not engine code. New tool → no renderer/flow change. The spec is validated at arm and dry-run once before it's live.

Detecting change — a ladder, best rung first

"Fire when it changes" has four implementations. We pick the highest rung the tool supports — automatically, per tool.

RungWhenHowCost
1 · subscribe tool/MCP advertises a stream or webhook register once; the tool pushes — zero polling, lowest latencybest
2 · cursor / CDC tool takes since/updated_after/etag ask only for what changed since the last cursor — no missed events, cheaplow
3 · poll + diff tool only returns a full list fetch, diff against the persisted key-set, fire the deltamedium
4 · threshold a value, not a list ("price", "queue depth") evaluate the predicate; fire on the crossing, not every tickmedium

Box-direct is already a live rung-3 poller — the generalization is proven, not speculative. Rung 1 is where MCP-native subscriptions make CUGA genuinely push, not poll.

Two watcher engines — cheap by default, smart on demand

default

Deterministic poll

The platform executes the WatchSpec: call tool → diff/threshold → fire. No LLM per tick. Predictable cost, predictable behavior. The right choice for 90% of watches.

Wakes the agent only when there's a real event to reason about.

opt-in

Agent-per-tick

For watches that need judgement to even detect ("tell me when the tone in the support queue turns angry"). The agent runs each tick, decides if it's an event. Costs an LLM call per interval — so it's opt-in and cadence-floored.

Same knob you already have for cron/poll — start deterministic, escalate to agent only when the detection itself is a reasoning task.

Reliability — the part AP was doing for us

Native watching means we own correctness. That's the real cost — not code volume. The guardrails, mostly patterns we already have:

Never miss

Durable next-fire in events.db + lazy catch-up — survives restarts, overshoots by at most one tick. (The bounded-run pattern, reused.)

Never double-fire

The key is the dedup identity; state persists per subscription. Re-arm and restart don't re-alert old items.

Never lie

Repeated tool errors → dead-letter with the last error surfaced in the Runs tab (status + flow-id already there). A stuck poller can't look like "watching".

Never runaway

Per-tool cadence floor, global concurrency cap, and a log()'d note on every skip — silent truncation reads as false coverage.

It reuses the whole spine — one new backend

Trigger rows already carry backend: ap | direct. Add backend: "tool". Everything downstream is untouched:

LayerWhat changes for tool-triggers
Trigger contractNothing — the poller POSTs the same normalized envelope to /invoke that an AP piece does. synth-fire tests it with no tool connected.
Agent / deliveryNothing — the agent answers, the result delivers to the same channels (web/Slack/Discord/Telegram).
Studio · RunsRows show integration=<tool>, backend=tool — same filters, same flow-id/status you can debug.
Concierge NL→FlowNew selector rung: intent the agent can watch with a tool → tool-poll backend, no AP. Sits beside cron / poll / push.

"Adding a tool-trigger" = a data row + a WatchSpec the agent authors. The gates, Studio, and this story update themselves.

Milestones — watch anything

#MilestoneProves
M1Poll-a-tool MVP — one ToolPoller (generalized box_direct), one example tool wired through /invoke with a synth-fire test."watch a non-AP tool, fire on change" — the event-driven claim becomes true.
M2Registry-driven + agent-authored — any tool becomes a trigger via a WatchSpec; NL→Flow arms it; Studio surfaces it.reach without code per tool.
M3Cursor / CDC + dry-run preview — incremental queries; "here's what it returns now" before arming (ask-till-legit).efficiency + no missed events + trust.
M4MCP-native subscribe — detect stream/webhook capability, prefer push over poll.genuinely push, not poll.

Each milestone ships alone. M1 is the smallest thing that makes "CUGA is event-driven" honest.

Part II

Events with & without AP,
in the cloud

AP is a backend you can add — not a dependency you're stuck with.

AP is a backend, not the spine

Everything already converges on one seam — /invoke. AP webhooks hit it. Direct channels hit it. The native poller hits it. synth-fire injects at it with AP not even running. That last fact is the proof: the trigger contract is backend-agnostic.

So AP earns its keep for exactly one thing — maintained OAuth connectors with token lifecycle (Gmail, Salesforce, the 754). It should never be the price of admission for a cron job, a webhook, or watching your own tool.

The capability report the server prints at boot already tiers this honestly — we're making the tiers real, not inventing them.

Three capability tiers

Tier 0 · zero AP

CUGA-only

  • web + webhook
  • direct channels (Slack, Discord)
  • native schedule (cron)
  • native poll (value watch)
  • tool-triggers (Part I)

Runs anywhere. No container. The resilient core.

Tier 1 · + AP

CUGA + Activepieces

  • everything in Tier 0
  • + 754 managed SaaS connectors
  • + OAuth token lifecycle (agent sees no creds)
  • + Telegram (AP webhook)

Add AP when you need a maintained connector — not before.

Tier 2 · cloud

Deployed CUGA + AP

  • real ingress (no cloudflared flap)
  • per-tenant isolation
  • managed secrets + domains
  • always-on, multi-user

From laptop demo to a product other people can use.

Events without AP — what you already get

Tier 0 is not a toy. With --events alone and no Activepieces at all, the platform watches, schedules, and acts:

  • Native scheduler — "every weekday at 8am", "every 15 min" run in-process. The most common trigger, with zero container. (Today this still borrows AP's schedule piece — the P0 is to bring it in-process with a durable next-fire.)
  • Native poll — "watch X every N and tell me on a change" — the agent re-runs its own tools. Already AP-free in the concierge.
  • Tool-triggers — Part I. Watch anything the agent can call.
  • Direct channels + webhook — Slack/Discord over their own transports; any system that can POST reaches /invoke.

The honest tradeoff: native means we own scheduling reliability (missed ticks, recovery) that AP gave us free — the guardrails from slide 8 are exactly that debt, paid.

Events with AP — when the weight is worth it

What AP uniquely brings

  • 754 pre-built, maintained connectors
  • the full OAuth dance + token refresh — the agent never touches a credential
  • battle-tested polling for SaaS webhooks

What it costs

  • a container stack (app + postgres + redis)
  • a public tunnel for inbound webhooks — the flaky part
  • an operational surface to run and secure

The rule: the concierge picks the lightest backend that satisfies the intent — webhook → native schedule → native poll / tool → AP only for a managed SaaS connector. AP is the fallback, never the default.

Cloud topology — and why it fixes today's pain

The #1 "everything stopped firing" cause today is the ephemeral cloudflared tunnel dying. A real deployment replaces it with proper ingress — the flakiness is a laptop artifact, not the architecture.

PieceLocal (today)Cloud (Tier 2)
CUGA servercuga start … --events on :7860container behind a load balancer, stable domain
Public URLngrok / cloudflared (flaps)managed ingress + TLS — no tunnel
Activepieceslocal podman stackdeployed service (or hosted AP), private network to CUGA
Stateevents.db (sqlite)managed Postgres — subscriptions, run log, watch state
Secrets.enva secrets manager; AP holds SaaS tokens, CUGA holds tool creds
Tenancysingle userper-tenant isolation — scope every flow, run, connection

Deployment shapes — one app, three homes

dev

Laptop

podman + tunnels + sqlite. make up. What we have. Great for building, wrong for "always on".

staging

Single VM / container host

CUGA + AP as containers, a real domain, Postgres. Always-on, one tenant. The first "someone else can use it" step.

prod

Cloud / managed

Orchestrated (k8s or a PaaS), managed Postgres + secrets + ingress, per-tenant isolation, autoscale the poll/agent workers.

The migration promise: the app doesn't change across homes. Same cuga start … --events, same /invoke, same registry. Only the infra around it — ingress, datastore, secrets — swaps. Deployment is a packaging problem, not a rewrite.

How the two bets sequence

PhaseBet I — watch anythingBet II — without-AP + cloud
Nowdone actions gated off — AP is trigger-only; CUGA owns toolsdone capability tiers are real in the boot report
NextM1 ToolPoller + one tool-trigger e2enative scheduler in-process (drop AP for cron)
ThenM2–M3 agent-authored WatchSpec + CDC + dry-runcontainerize CUGA+AP, real ingress, Postgres state
LaterM4 MCP-native subscribe (true push)per-tenant isolation + managed secrets → multi-user cloud

Both threads pull toward the same claim: CUGA watches anything, runs anywhere, and only leans on AP when a managed SaaS connector is genuinely the best tool.

The finish line

A customer says "keep an eye on this" — and it doesn't matter whether "this" is Gmail, their own service, or a tool they wrote this morning. The agent finds the way to watch it, and it runs in the cloud whether or not Activepieces is in the picture.

That's what makes it a platform, not an integration list.
